Unsurprisingly, the country is one of the most competitive bookmaker markets on the continent, with more than thirty licensed sports betting and online-gaming brands fighting for attention.

Know the Rules: GBT Licensing and the 12% Tax

The Gaming Board of Tanzania is the sole authority for issuing gambling licences and supervising operators through its online registers. Any bookmaker accepting TZS deposits from players inside Tanzania is expected to hold a valid GBT betting or online-gaming licence, and the board publishes licensed regist. The practical check for punters is simple: open the site footer, confirm the licence, then cross-check the brand against the GBT list published at gamingboard.go.tz.

Winnings are taxed at source. The Tanzania Revenue Authority applies a 12% withholding on sports-betting winnings and 15% on casino winnings, so the figure shown on your bet slip is pre-tax. Odds quotes and promotions are still competitive across the licensed field, but always run the post-tax maths before comparing brands on advertised value.

Licence check: brands such as Betway (Media Bay Ltd), SportPesa (Nexis Global), 1xBet (Katavi Gaming), Betika (Paladin & Associates), BetPawa (Choplife Gaming) and SportyBet (Marawin Ltd) all appear on current GBT betting registers. Yet the sector is split across multiple laws and institutions, casinos are licensed separately by the Ministry of Tourism, and a wave of offshore brands with Curacao licences still serve Zambian players.

Winnings also carry a 15% withholding tax. That means the operator, not you, absorbs the levy, but payout speed and terms matter more than ever when real money is moving both directions.

h1: Best Betting Sites in Pakistan 2026: The Honest Guide to the Legal Landscape
lead: Pakistan is often called the world's largest unregulated cricket betting market, but there is nothing about it that a review site should celebrate: gambling is prohibited, sites are blocked, and offshore operators offer no legal protection. Here is the honest 2026 picture.
thumbCaption: The honest picture of betting sites in Pakistan in 2026
share: There are no legal betting sites in Pakistan. This guide explains the 1977 gambling ban, PTA site blocks, the 2025 app crackdown, and the real risks of offshore cricket-betting platforms.
content:
Before listing anything, the truth: Pakistan has no legal online betting sites, no licensed sportsbooks, and no regulator issuing betting licences. Gambling is prohibited under the Prevention of Gambling Act of 1977, reinforced by the Pakistan Penal Code and by Article 37(g) of the Constitution, which directs the state to prevent gambling in line with Islamic principles (maisir).

Yet by volume of money, Pakistan is one of the largest betting markets on earth. Analysts estimate the country's cricket betting handle at around $2.1 billion a year, driven overwhelmingly by the Pakistan Super League and the IPL, which draws an estimated 55 million Pakistani viewers per major fixture. That demand is served entirely by offshore platforms that operate in a legal grey zone, with no domestic protection for players.

If you are hunting for a best-betting-site list for Pakistan, the honest answer is that no list can recommend a legal site. What we can do is explain the law, what enforcement looks like in 2026, which platforms dominate the grey market, and the real risks you take by using them.

PaymentsJazzCash and Easypaisa agents (officially prohibited for betting), USDT-TRC20 crypto P2P, bank cards mostly blocked
Main betting driverCricket — PSL and IPL season peaks

Know the Rules: A 1977 Law in a 2026 World

The Prevention of Gambling Act 1977 was written for physical gaming houses and has never been amended for the internet. That creates a grey zone: there is no specific statute saying using a betting app is a crime, but gambling itself is prohibited, and the state treats digital gambling as a serious enforcement matter.

Penalties on the books include fines and up to a year's imprisonment for operating a gambling facility, fines of up to Rs 5,000 and one year for participating in a common gaming house, and heavier cyber-crime charges under the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act (PECA) 2016 for hosting or promoting gambling apps. In practice, documented prosecutions target operators, promoters and money handlers, not individual bettors using apps on personal phones. That has not protected the industry from a serious clampdown.

August 2025 crackdown: the NCCIA declared 46 mobile apps illegal and ordered the PTA to block them nationwide, including Bet365, 1xBet, Betway, Dafabet, 22Bet, Melbet, Parimatch, 10Cric, Betwinner, 888Starz and Thunderpick, plus forex platforms. Enforcement also ramped up in 2025 with 150 JazzCash agents detained, PKR 200 million frozen in gambling-linked accounts, and dozens of bank accounts suspended.

The Grey Market: What Pakistani Bettors Actually Use

Because no domestic option exists, bettors turn offshore. The platforms that dominate Pakistani cricket wagering are Curacao- or Gibraltar-licensed international brands: 1xBet, bet365, Parimatch, Melbet, 22Bet, 10Cric, Stake and Dafabet. Some hold strong overseas licences; several were named in the August 2025 NCCIA ban and blocked at ISP level, so access now typically requires a VPN and mirror domains.

It is important to say plainly what betting on these platforms means in Pakistan in 2026: none is licensed to take Pakistani customers, none answers to a Pakistani authority, and the State Bank of Pakistan restricts banks from processing gambling transactions. If a site refuses a withdrawal, freezes an account, or shuts down, your only recourse is the company and its foreign regulator. Reputable Malta-licensed operators, by contrast, actively block Pakistani registrations because their own rules forbid accepting players from jurisdictions where gambling is illegal.

How Payments Work in the Grey Market

Bank cards are largely unusable because banks refuse gambling merchant codes. Two workarounds dominate. The first is mobile wallets: JazzCash and Easypaisa have tens of millions of registered accounts, and while both explicitly prohibit gambling transactions in their terms, deposits are routed through third-party agents who convert cash. The second is crypto: P2P exchanges and USDT-TRC20 wallets, often with a 3-5% conversion spread, are the more anonymous route. In March 2026 Pakistan passed the Virtual Assets Act, bringing crypto under a regulatory framework, so the monitoring landscape is still settling.

Every one of these routes carries risk: wallet flags and freezes, FIA account inquiries on larger transfers, VPN data exposure, and the near-total absence of dispute protection.

The Legal and Financial Risks, Straight

Betting from Pakistan in 2026 means betting without a license, without a regulator, without an ombudsman and frequently without a stable connection to your own money. Sites vanish or swap domains without notice. Large wins can trigger source-of-funds checks that freeze payments for months. If a platform becomes unreachable, your balance goes with it. And the enforcement environment is tightening, not relaxing, with AI-driven monitoring of gambling-linked transfers and new crypto rules.

Gambling will not be legalised here any time soon; religious and constitutional constraints make that politically near-impossible in the 2026-2028 window.

If You Still Bet: The Minimum Precautions

We cannot advise using illegal offshore platforms. If you make that choice anyway, the minimum sensible precautions are: use accounts in your own verified name only, never share PINs or OTPs, keep stakes small and within what you can afford to lose, hold records of every transaction, and understand that you have fundamentally no legal protection if the operator refuses to pay.

Responsible Gambling in Pakistan

There is no national gambling helpline because gambling is illegal. If betting stops being entertainment, the most powerful public health lever available to Pakistani players is simply to stop: the enforcement regime does that itself, and the safest bet in Pakistan is the one never placed. Never chase losses, never borrow to gamble, and if you or someone you know is struggling with betting behaviour, seek professional mental-health support.

h1: Best Betting Sites in Bangladesh 2026: The Gambling Prevention Act — What Bettors Must Know
lead: Bangladesh ended 159 years of legal ambiguity on 1 July 2026: the Gambling Prevention Act puts online betting, VPN use and betting-linked mobile money behind prison bars. There are no legal betting sites in Bangladesh, and the honest 2026 answer to most betting questions now starts and ends with the law.
thumbCaption: Bangladesh's new gambling law changes everything for bettors in 2026
share: Bangladesh's Gambling Prevention Act 2026 makes online betting a serious crime — up to 7 years in jail and Tk 5 crore fines. Here is what bettors need to know.
content:
On 1 July 2026, Bangladesh replaced the colonial-era Public Gambling Act of 1867 with the Gambling Prevention Act 2026 (Act No. 98 of 2026). It is the most significant gambling law reform in the country's history, and it closes the loophole offshore betting platforms had been exploiting for years. There are now explicitly no legal online betting sites in Bangladesh, and the penalties are severe enough to change the calculation for anyone tempted to use one.

Bangladesh was never a safe market for offshore betting, but the grey area is gone. Under the 1867 act a judge once had to decide whether a website counted as a common gaming house. Under the 2026 act, online gambling has its own chapter of offences, its own dedicated tribunal, and its own financial-crime machinery.

This guide walks through the new law, the penalties, how the grey market got here, and why the honest answer to best-betting-site questions about Bangladesh in 2026 is a legal one.

Bangladesh Betting at a Glance

FactorDetail
CurrencyBangladeshi taka (BDT / Tk)
Governing lawGambling Prevention Act 2026 (Act No. 98 of 2026), in force 1 July 2026
Legal online bettingNone — sports betting, online betting, exchange and casino wagers all prohibited

VPN / mirror / proxyCriminalised when used to access or facilitate gambling platforms
EnforcementCyber Tribunal jurisdiction; MFS and crypto wallets can be frozen; 55,000+ gambling-linked accounts already frozen
Main betting driverCricket — Bangladesh Premier League and national-team fixtures

Know the Rules: What the 2026 Act Actually Does

The Gambling Prevention Act 2026 defines gambling activities in 24 categories, from sports betting and live betting to exchange betting, virtual betting, fantasy and e-sports. It names cryptocurrencies (Bitcoin, Ethereum, USDT), digital wallets and NFTs as instruments of prohibited gambling, and it treats gambling-linked money transfers as predicate offences under the Money Laundering Prevention Act 2012. The penalties are tiered by proximity to the crime:

  • Basic gambling: up to 2 years' imprisonment and fines up to Tk 200,000
  • Online or remote gambling: up to 5 years and fines up to Tk 1 crore
  • Placing bets online: up to 7 years and fines up to Tk 5 crore

The law also criminalises running gambling platforms through VPNs, proxies, mirror sites, hosting, domains and CDNs, requires ISPs to block identified gambling platforms, and gives authorities the power to freeze bank accounts, MFS accounts, digital wallets and crypto wallets linked to gambling.

Enforcement context: enforcement was building before Parliament acted. In May 2025 the CID identified more than 1,000 mobile-banking agents involved in gambling transactions and referred them to Bangladesh Bank, and by mid-2026 the financial intelligence unit had frozen around 55,000 Mobile Financial Service accounts connected to online gambling and digital hundi operations.

How the Grey Market Got Here

For years Bangladesh's betting culture — dominated by cricket, the Bangladesh Premier League and the national team — ran through offshore platforms such as bet365, Betway, 1xBet, Parimatch, Melbet and 10Cric. Users registered with VPNs, funded accounts through bKash, Nagad and Rocket agents, and largely escaped the 1867 act because its language could not reach the internet. Rough estimates suggested around 5 million people engaged in online gambling in Bangladesh, with roughly USD 450 million flowing out through informal channels.

That era is over. bKash and Nagad both officially prohibit gambling transactions, agents who facilitate them face licence cancellations and proceedings, and since 1 July 2026 every link in the chain — platform, VPN, host, agent, payment account — is individually addressable by the new law.

What Offshore Sites Are Used in Bangladesh

The brands Bangladeshi bettors historically turned to are the same global names seen across South Asia: bet365 and Betway for streaming and European football depth, 1xBet and Parimatch for the deepest cricket and league markets, and Melbet or 10Cric for cricket-led offers. For the record: none of these holds any authorisation to serve Bangladeshi customers; betting through them is an offence under the 2026 Act; and the practical risk of doing so has increased materially — accounts can be frozen, agents arrested, and participants prosecuted.

The Risks, Straight

Since 1 July 2026, betting online in Bangladesh means risking up to seven years' imprisonment and a Tk 5 crore fine. Using a VPN to reach a gambling platform is itself criminalised. Your MFS wallet, bank account or crypto wallet can be frozen on suspicion. There is no licensed operator and no domestic dispute process — a refused withdrawal leaves you with nothing but a foreign licence that has no standing in Bangladesh.

Responsible Gambling in Bangladesh

There is no national gambling helpline in Bangladesh because gambling is illegal. The 2026 law allocates no space for rehabilitation, awareness or treatment. The only responsible guidance we can give is the law's own: the safest position for a Bengali bettor in 2026 is not to bet. If betting has become a problem in someone's life, professional mental-health and counselling services, not offshore platforms, are the right referral.

faqs.q: Is online betting legal in Bangladesh?
faqs.a: No. The Gambling Prevention Act 2026 (Act No. 98 of 2026), in force since 1 July 2026, prohibits sports betting, online betting, exchange and casino wagers, and repeals the old Public Gambling Act 1867.

faqs.q: What are the penalties under the new law?
faqs.a: Placing bets online carries up to 7 years' imprisonment and fines up to Tk 5 crore. Running online or remote gambling carries up to 5 years and fines up to Tk 1 crore, and basic gambling up to 2 years and Tk 200,000.

faqs.q: Can using a VPN to bet get me in trouble?
faqs.a: Yes. The 2026 Act explicitly criminalises the use of VPNs, proxies, mirror sites, hosting, domains and CDNs to access or facilitate gambling platforms, and requires ISPs to block identified gambling sites.

faqs.q: Can my bKash or Nagad account be frozen?
faqs.a: Yes. Authorities may freeze MFS accounts, digital wallets and crypto wallets linked to gambling, and around 55,000 mobile financial service accounts linked to gambling were frozen in 2025-26.

faqs.q: Are there any legal options for sports betting in Bangladesh?
faqs.a: No. There is no licensed sportsbook, no legal online betting and no domestic dispute process. The only lawful position under the 2026 Act is not to bet.

There is also a lesser-known rule that shapes how you play: under Acuerdo 08, you must stake at least 50% of your deposits before you can withdraw. Budget it into your bankroll and always confirm the terms at your chosen operator.

The illegal world is everything else — offshore brands marketing to Filipino players with no local licence, most of which are blocked by the NTC.

The line between them became much clearer in 2024-2025 when President Marcos Jr. ordered the total shutdown of Philippine Offshore Gaming Operators (POGOs) after years of scandals involving fraud, money laundering and human trafficking. Know the Rules: PAGCOR Licensing and the POGO Ban

PAGCOR derives its power from Presidential Decree 1869 and Republic Act 9487 (franchise extended to 2033) and licenses domestic online casinos, e-bingo and sports betting for play within the Philippines. The number of online gaming licensees has consolidated from 74 to 48, with a moratorium on new licences in place since March 2024 while PAGCOR pushes the industry to consolidate. Authorised operators must comply with KYC, self-exclusion and responsible-marketing obligations, and PAGCOR works with the NTC to block illegal sites — more than 3,000 were IP-blocked as of mid-2025.

In 2025 the PlaySafe Alliance of the Philippines was founded by leading PAGCOR-licensed operators to strengthen compliance, responsible gaming and consumer protection across the licensed market.

Legally, Cameroon is stricter than many African markets. Online betting is regulated by the Ministry of Territorial Administration (MINAT) under Law 2015/012 and Decree 2019/2300/PM. Legitimate online operators must hold a MINAT authorisation, be locally incorporated, run .cm domains, and route all payments through the state-designated aggregator InTouch Cameroun (mandatory since 30 January 2025).

Know the Rules: MINAT Authorisation and the InTouch Switch

Online operators in Cameroon need a MINAT authorisation, a locally incorporated Cameroonian company (Sarl or SA) and a .cm domain. Verify any site by scanning the footer for a licence number in the format n XXXXXX/A/MINAT/SG/DAP/SDLP/SJ and matching the named entity to the company on your deposit receipt. There is no single public registry, so the operator's own published footer is the primary check.

On 30 January 2025 MINAT enforced an exclusive payments contract with InTouch Cameroun. Deposits that had been paid straight from MTN MoMo or Orange Money to operator wallets were briefly blocked, and brands like betPawa, 1xBet, Betwinner and Betmomo had to re-route; most restored service within days. Since then, all legal betting payments flow through InTouch. From 1 January 2026, offshore operators serving Cameroonian players without local authorisation also face a 3% turnover tax and growing enforcement scrutiny.
